properties.name: Natural deduction records honestly: a proof by cases can name an assumed disjunction, a rule is the step's rule (not a premise), one formula can recur under different suppositions, a premise can be used twice, each line can say whether it shows ⊨ or ⊢, and a theorem reads which part stands
properties.statement:
From the logic rung (2026-10-19, e104c2efbcc0fb6d, 0.88.0):
1. cases_exhaustive can name a disjunction ASSUMED in the same subproof; it is read as assumed there, not by its standing status.
2. A step's rule is a first-class reference (to a rule node), so a what-if on a rule reaches its steps without listing the rule as a premise.
3. The same formula under different suppositions need not be a new node each time (⊥ was recorded twenty times).
4. A premise can be used twice in one step (A, A ⊢ A∧A).
5. A line of support can say what relation it establishes (semantic ⊨ by truth table, derivability ⊢ by deduction).
6. A theorem that is a conjunction or biconditional reads which part stands after a what-if.
7. A step resting on an unverified citation reads conditional at the step, not only at the claim; and the independence check also compares shared cited foundations, not only shared steps.
